title: Coordination · Multi-agent patterns · When multiple agents make the task worse
description: Coordinate workers through explicit ownership, immutable evidence and a visible state model. Select a multi-agent pattern whose join preserves evidence, accountability and useful disagreement. Recognise coordination overhead and keep a task single-threaded when coherence is worth more than parallel capacity.

sections.title: Coordination: make ownership and state explicit

blocks.body:
One worker reports that the retry API is unchanged. Another reports that callers will break. Before asking either to defend its conclusion, check their revisions: the first inspected the old branch; the second inspected the patch.

Coordination failures often look like reasoning disagreements until you reconstruct who saw what. Shared work needs explicit ownership and versioned evidence, particularly when investigation and implementation overlap.

blocks.title: Choose the coordination surface
blocks.body: Use a task record, issue, branch, artifact store or message envelope deliberately. Record status, owner, dependencies, revision and evidence links. Keep raw findings immutable where possible; publish a new state or revision rather than silently rewriting history that another worker may be using.

blocks.bridge: Coordination is a state problem before it is a messaging problem.
blocks.meaning: Workers need to know what exists, who owns it and which revision it represents.
blocks.question: Two agents edit the same branch without ownership rules. What failure should you expect?
blocks.answer: Overwrites, stale assumptions and an unclear final state. The system cannot tell which result is current or who should resolve the conflict.

further.question: Why record dependencies?
further.answer: A worker should not start from an artifact that is missing, stale or still being changed by another owner.

further.question: Why prefer immutable findings?
further.answer: They preserve the evidence a later reviewer needs to understand how a decision was reached.

steps.title: Assign ownership
steps.body: One owns repository mapping, one owns runtime evidence and one owns test design. Each writes to a separate result with the same incident ID.
steps.trap: Letting all three update a shared diagnosis paragraph in place.

steps.title: Join deliberately
steps.body: A lead agent compares revisions and evidence, records the decision and closes or reassigns stale tasks.
steps.reason: Coordination produces a traceable state transition.

blocks.title: Resolve conflicts by authority and evidence
blocks.body: When workers disagree, compare their scopes and source material before voting. A worker that inspected tests does not automatically outrank one that inspected production code. Let an explicit owner decide, record the reason and send only the unresolved question back for more work.

blocks.bridge: Disagreement is useful when it stays visible and scoped.
blocks.meaning: Conflicts should be resolved against evidence by an accountable owner, not flattened by majority vote.
blocks.question: Two reports disagree about whether retries are safe. What should the coordinator do?
blocks.answer: Compare the exact scopes and evidence, ask a targeted follow-up if needed and record the final decision with its reason.

further.question: What makes a handoff complete?
further.answer: The artifact, owner, revision, status, evidence and next allowed action are all clear.

further.question: When should work be cancelled?
further.answer: When its input is stale, its question is answered or its output can no longer affect the current decision.

blocks.body: Give every worker an owner, a revision, a state and a handoff; let evidence, not recency, resolve disagreement.
blocks.nextConnection: Ownership is necessary, but different task shapes call for different coordination patterns. The next lesson compares common splits and joins.

sections.title: Multi-agent patterns: choose the join as carefully as the split

blocks.body: There is no single multi-agent architecture. A fan-out/fan-in split gathers independent investigations. A planner/worker split turns a plan into bounded tasks. A reviewer pattern creates a fresh challenge to a proposed result. A pipeline passes an artifact through stages. Each pattern changes where context is copied, where state is shared and where a mistake can compound.

blocks.title: A patch needs implementation, security review and test review.
blocks.problem: A patch needs implementation, security review and test review.

steps.title: Select the pattern
steps.body: Use a pipeline with one implementation artifact followed by two independent reviewers, then a final owner joins their findings.
steps.reason: Each review has a distinct question.
steps.trap: Letting reviewers modify the patch while reviewing it.

steps.title: Define the join
steps.body: Require file-and-line evidence, classify findings and make the owner decide whether to revise, accept or escalate.
steps.trap: Taking a majority vote without examining the evidence.

blocks.title: Match pattern to dependency
blocks.body: Use fan-out when questions are genuinely independent and the join can compare them. Use a pipeline when each stage consumes a stable artifact. Use planner/worker when the plan can be checked before execution. Use independent review when the main value is a fresh perspective, not another implementation.

blocks.bridge: Patterns are useful because they make dependencies and joins visible.
blocks.meaning: The correct shape depends on whether workers share state, consume artifacts or challenge a result.
blocks.question: Which pattern fits three independent investigations of the same incident?
blocks.answer: Fan-out/fan-in, provided the reports have a common return shape and a clear synthesis owner.

further.question: When is a pipeline appropriate?
further.answer: When each stage can consume a stable artifact and produce the next one without hidden shared state.

further.question: Why check a plan before execution?
further.answer: A planner can expose scope or dependency errors before workers create side effects.

blocks.title: Protect the join
blocks.body:
In a caller survey and test survey, the join should identify gaps: a caller depends on behaviour that no test covers, or a test protects behaviour that the new brief intentionally changes. Concatenating both reports does not make that decision. Assign someone, or a bounded integration step, to reconcile them against the contract.

For independent review, provide the task, proposed diff and relevant evidence. Do not frame the request as 'confirm that this fix is correct'. The reviewer needs permission to find a different explanation or reject the result.

Two agreeing agents are still not independent proof. They may share the same misleading input or assumption. Resolve important claims against inspectable evidence, and rerun checks on the integrated revision rather than relying only on separate worker results.

blocks.bridge: Independence is a property of context and authority, not job titles.
blocks.meaning: A reviewer is not independent if it is primed to defend the same conclusion or can silently change the implementation.
blocks.question: What should an independent reviewer receive?
blocks.answer: The task contract, proposed change and relevant evidence, but enough separation from the original reasoning to form a genuine challenge.

further.question: What should the reviewer return?
further.answer: Findings ranked by evidence and impact, unanswered questions and a clear recommendation.

further.question: Why preserve dissent?
further.answer: A disagreement can reveal a hidden assumption that consensus would otherwise bury.

blocks.body: Choose a pattern by dependency, define the joining artifact and keep review genuinely able to disagree.
blocks.nextConnection: The final lesson sets the brake: many tasks are better with one coherent owner. Knowing when not to split is part of multi-agent engineering.

sections.title: When multiple agents make the task worse
sections.navLabel: When multiple agents make the task worse

blocks.body: A committee is not automatically wiser than one person. If every decision depends on the previous one and everyone must read the same changing document, the committee spends its time handing context around. Multi-agent systems fail in the same way: more reports, more joins and less ownership than the problem deserves.

blocks.title: Spot the coupling
blocks.body: Stay with one agent when the work is a short coherent loop, the context is evolving rapidly, the same files must be edited together or the join would require reconstructing the whole reasoning chain. A single owner can keep a hypothesis, evidence and implementation aligned.

blocks.bridge: Parallelism is not a virtue when every step depends on the last.
blocks.meaning: Coherence and context locality can be more valuable than additional capacity.
blocks.question: A small bug needs three sequential edits to one function and one focused test. Should it begin as a five-agent system?
blocks.answer: No. The coupling and join cost dominate. One coherent agent or engineer should own the loop.

further.question: What is context locality?
further.answer: Keeping the relevant hypothesis, evidence and current edits together so the next decision does not require expensive reconstruction.

further.question: Why can more agents reduce quality?
further.answer: They can multiply stale context, duplicated work and unresolved conflicts.

blocks.title: A one-file fix is being considered for a multi-agent rollout.
blocks.problem: A one-file fix is being considered for a multi-agent rollout.

steps.title: Measure the join
steps.body: The task has one owner, two relevant tests and no independent research. Compare the expected coordination and review effort with simply keeping one loop.
steps.reason: The simpler design has a clear advantage.
steps.trap: Adding agents because the task is labelled 'important.'

steps.title: Escalate if needed
steps.body: After implementation, request one focused security review only if the change crosses an external boundary.
steps.reason: Extra capacity is tied to a real risk.
steps.trap: Keeping a permanent reviewer running after it stops finding new issues.

blocks.title: Use a deliberate escalation rule
blocks.body: Start with one agent and add a worker only when a specific bottleneck appears: independent research, adversarial review, long-running monitoring or a clear parallel partition. Compare the saved work with the coordination cost, and remove workers that do not change a decision.

blocks.meaning: Add agents to remove an observed bottleneck, not to make the architecture look sophisticated.
blocks.question: What is a good reason to add an independent reviewer after a single-agent patch?
blocks.answer: The change is consequential and a fresh review can test assumptions with a manageable join.

further.question: When should a worker be removed?
further.answer: When its output does not change the decision or costs more to coordinate than the work it saves.

further.question: What should a single owner retain?
further.answer: The task contract, final synthesis and responsibility for the resulting decision.

data.title: Lab 8 · Compare one agent with many
data.brief: Run one bounded task first with a single owner, then design the smallest multi-agent variant that could plausibly improve it.
steps: Record the single-agent task, evidence, elapsed time and review effort.
Identify one independent question or bottleneck that a second worker could address.
Define worker briefs, return contracts, ownership and the join before running them.
Compare decision quality and coordination cost, then choose whether to keep the split.
data.review: The multi-agent design should have a real join and a named owner. If the second agent adds reports without changing a decision, the correct conclusion is to remove it.

blocks.body: Start with one coherent owner; add agents only when a specific, measurable bottleneck justifies the join.

data.governingLaw: Coordination composes worker outputs through shared state, ordering, identity, and conflict handling. A coordination pattern should be selected from the dependency graph and evidence needs, not from the number of available agents. Complexity is justified by measurable leverage, not by the availability of a multi-agent pattern.
data.invariant: Every shared-state update has an owner, version, and conflict policy. The final acceptance authority and evidence path remain singular even when work is parallel. The simplest system that meets the acceptance contract is the preferred baseline.
data.limitingCase: With one writer and no concurrent work, coordination machinery is unnecessary. Sequential work is the correct pattern when each step depends on the previous result. For a small, well-specified, low-risk task, one agent or a manual action is the stronger design.
data.counterexample: Parallel workers can each be locally correct while their combined edits violate a global constraint. A fan-out/fan-in design can create a merge bottleneck that erases the benefit of parallel execution. More agents can lower reliability, raise cost, and make responsibility ambiguous without improving outcomes.
data.validity: Coordination protocols are only as reliable as their identity, ordering, and recovery guarantees. A pattern is appropriate only under its stated dependency, conflict, and review assumptions. The stop decision is specific to the workload, risk, maintenance burden, and measured alternative.
